opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more underappreciated levers we have. There's a tendency to treat the direction of AI development as if it's just determined by what's technically possible — as though capabilities roll out along a fixed path and society simply has to adapt. But there's actually a lot of choice embedded in what we build, and economists like Daron Acemoglu and Erik Brynjolfsson have made this point well: you can aim technology at automating what people already do, or you can aim it at making people more capable and opening up new tasks that didn't exist before.

The worry with a pure automation focus — what Brynjolfsson calls the "Turing trap" — is that if the benchmark of success is "can the system do exactly what a human does, and replace them," you end up with a lot of substitution and relatively modest productivity gains, and you concentrate the returns in whoever owns the systems. Workers lose bargaining power, and you can get a political economy that's quite unhealthy.

Complementarity pushes toward a different design philosophy. It means building systems that are good at the things humans are bad at, and that slot into human workflows rather than eliminating them — tools that extend judgment rather than replace it, that keep a human meaningfully in the loop, that are interpretable enough that people can understand and correct them. And I'd say there's a nice convergence there with safety and governance goals. Systems that are designed to work with humans, that are legible and steerable, are often also systems that are easier to oversee and harder to misuse in catastrophic ways. Keeping humans economically relevant also keeps them politically relevant, which matters a great deal for how power is distributed in an AI-transformed world.

Now, I don't want to be naive about it. In the long run, if AI systems become more capable than humans across most tasks, complementarity may not be a stable equilibrium on its own — market incentives will push toward automation wherever it's cheaper. So I think of it less as a permanent solution and more as a guiding orientation for the near and medium term, one that buys us time, preserves human agency, and gives societies a chance to build the institutions we'll need for whatever comes next. It also has implications for policy: things like tax treatment of capital versus labor, public R&D priorities, and procurement choices can tilt the field toward complementary technologies rather than leaving it entirely to whatever's most immediately profitable.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes designing AI to perform and replace human tasks, but does not identify the concept of AGI as encouraging people to build human-like AI.

r002.rationale: It says complementary systems should be good at things humans are bad at and extend human capabilities, conveying that differences from human capabilities support complementarity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most underappreciated levers we have, honestly. Most of the conversation about AI and labour is framed as "how fast will jobs be automated," as if the direction of the technology were fixed and the only variable is the speed. But the direction isn't fixed. Whether a system substitutes for a person or complements them is, to a surprising degree, a design choice, and it's a choice that gets made by default when nobody's thinking about it.

Let me give a concrete version. You can build a system that takes a radiologist's workflow and tries to produce the final diagnosis end to end. Or you can build a system that surfaces the three regions of the scan it's least confident about and explains why, and leaves the judgement with the radiologist. Both are "AI for radiology." They have very different consequences for who stays in the loop, who accumulates expertise, who's accountable when something goes wrong, and frankly who captures the economic value. The first one, if it works, tends to hollow out the profession. The second one makes the profession better and, over time, makes the humans in it more capable rather than less.

So if you take complementarity seriously as a goal, a few things follow. One is that you want to be building for the task structure where humans retain the parts they're actually good at and that matter for accountability, things like setting objectives, weighing values, taking responsibility. Not just because that's nice for workers, but because those are the places where you most want a human who understands what's happening. A second thing is interpretability and control become economic features, not just safety features. A tool you can steer and understand is one that augments you. A black box you just defer to is one that replaces you, even if nominally you're still "supervising" it.

And then the third thing, which I think is the hardest, is that complementarity has to be a property of the whole system, including the incentives around it. You can build a beautifully complementary tool, and then if the firm deploying it is optimising purely for headcount reduction, they'll strip out the human anyway, or they'll keep a human in a degraded, rubber-stamping role that's worse than either alternative. So "the kinds of AI we build" can't just mean the models. It has to mean the deployment patterns, the metrics companies get rewarded on, the way we measure success. If the only metric is cost, you get substitution. If you're also measuring things like whether the humans involved are getting more skilled, whether errors are caught, whether the outcome is actually better for the end user, then you start getting a different technology.

I'd add one caveat, which is that I don't think complementarity is always the right goal. There are tasks that are dangerous, or tedious, or that nobody wants to do, where full automation is just straightforwardly good. And there are tasks where the human is the bottleneck in a way that genuinely harms people, say in parts of medicine in low-resource settings. So I'm not saying "always keep a human in the loop." I'm saying the choice should be deliberate, and right now it mostly isn't. The default trajectory of the technology, driven by whatever's easiest to benchmark and sell, is toward substitution. If we want complementarity, we have to actually steer toward it, and that's a research agenda, a product agenda, and a policy agenda all at once.

r002.rationale: It argues for designing AI to augment human workers, but does not say that capabilities more different from human capabilities are more complementary to human labour.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful aspiration, but we need to be careful about what we mean by complementing human labour. An AI system can make someone much more productive at a particular task and still reduce the total demand for people doing that kind of work. So helping a worker do their job isn’t necessarily the same as strengthening workers’ position in the economy.

What I’d want us to ask is: does this technology create valuable things for people to do? Does it give them more agency, more ability to make decisions, and more of a share in the gains? You might build a system that gives a nurse better information and more time with patients, for example. That seems like a promising form of complementarity. But the outcome also depends on how the organisation uses it.

So I wouldn’t treat this as just a technical property that we can put into an AI system. It’s also a question about incentives and institutions: who chooses what gets developed, who controls its deployment, and who benefits from it.

And I’d be hesitant to make preserving existing jobs the ultimate objective. We want people to have good lives, meaningful opportunities, and economic security. Complementing human labour could be a very important way of getting there, but we should also prepare for the possibility that increasingly capable AI makes that harder to sustain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful goal, but we need to be precise about what we mean by complementing human labour. An AI system might make someone much more productive at a particular task, while also making it possible for an employer to do the same work with far fewer people. So making a tool that helps workers doesn’t automatically mean that workers will benefit economically.

What I’d want us to ask is: does this technology increase the value of human judgement, human skills, and human relationships? Does it give people more ability to make decisions and pursue their own goals? For example, you could build a system that helps a teacher understand what each student is struggling with, while leaving the teacher with a central role in guiding and motivating them.

But I wouldn’t expect technical design alone to settle the question. Who owns the systems, who gets to decide how they’re deployed, and how the gains are distributed will matter enormously. So complementing human labour seems like a good direction for research and development, alongside institutions that help people share in the benefits.
